q014.stem:
You have an Azure SQL database that contains sales transactions and is updated frequently. You need to generate reports to detect fraudulent transactions. The data must be visible within five minutes of an update.

How should you configure the data connection?
options: Add a SQL statement.
Set the Command timeout in minutes setting.
Set Data Connectivity mode to Import.
Set Data Connectivity mode to DirectQuery.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Set Data Connectivity mode to DirectQuery.

Why it is correct: DirectQuery queries the source on every interaction, so changes show up as soon as the visual refreshes — well under five minutes and without waiting for a scheduled refresh.

  • Official documentation: DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Add a SQL statement. — Why it is incorrect: a SQL statement only changes which data is retrieved, not how fresh it is.
  • Option B — Set the Command timeout in minutes setting. — Why it is incorrect: the timeout only limits how long a query may run; it does not make data fresher.
  • Option C — Set Data Connectivity mode to Import. — Why it is incorrect: Import stores a cached copy refreshed only on schedule (max 8/day on Pro), so it cannot guarantee five minutes. Official documentation: Data refresh in Power BI - Microsoft Learn

q015.stem:
You have a folder that contains 100 CSV files. You need to make the file metadata available as a single dataset by using Power BI. The solution must NOT store the data of the CSV files.

Which three actions should you perform, and in what order?

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: From Power BI Desktop, select Get Data, and then select Folder.
  • Step 2: From Power Query Editor, remove the Content column.
  • Step 3: From Power Query Editor, expand the Attributes column.
  1. Get Data → Folder: the Folder connector returns one row per file with its metadata (name, extension, dates, path) and a Content column holding the binary.
  2. Remove the Content column: it holds the CSV data; removing it satisfies “must NOT store the data”.
  3. Expand the Attributes column: unfolds the extra metadata (size, dates…).

Combining the Content column would load the CSV data, the opposite of the requirement; Text/CSV opens a single file.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source key is Folder → expand Attributes → combine Content, but combining Content would load the CSV data, contradicting the statement; the community majority proposes Folder → remove Content → expand Attributes, which is what is shown here. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Folder connector - Microsoft Learn | Combine files overview - Microsoft Learn

q016.stem:
A BI developer creates a Power BI dataflow that uses DirectQuery to access tables from an on-premises SQL Server. The Enhanced Dataflows Compute Engine is on.

You need to use the dataflow in a report and: minimize online processing operations; minimize calculation and render times for visuals; include data from the current year up to and including the previous day. What should you do?
options: Create a dataflows connection that has DirectQuery mode selected.
Create a dataflows connection that has DirectQuery mode selected and configure a gateway connection for the dataset.
Create a dataflows connection that has Import mode selected and schedule a daily refresh.
Create a dataflows connection that has Import mode selected and create a Power Automate solution to refresh the data hourly.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Create a dataflows connection that has Import mode selected and schedule a daily refresh.

Why it is correct: Import caches the data in the model: visuals respond fast and there are no online queries. A daily refresh brings the report up to the previous day, exactly what is required, without the overhead of more frequent refreshes.

  • Official documentation: Premium features of dataflows - Microsoft Learn | Data refresh in Power BI - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Create a dataflows connection that has DirectQuery mode selected. — Why it is incorrect: DirectQuery over the dataflow causes online processing on every interaction, against the requirements.
  • Option B — Create a dataflows connection that has DirectQuery mode selected and configure a gateway connection for the dataset. — Why it is incorrect: it adds a gateway and is still DirectQuery: more online processing and slower.
  • Option D — Create a dataflows connection that has Import mode selected and create a Power Automate solution to refresh the data hourly. — Why it is incorrect: refreshing hourly is unnecessary (up to the previous day is enough), increases processing and adds Power Automate complexity.

q017.stem:
You publish a dataset that contains data from an on-premises SQL Server database. The dataset must be refreshed daily.

You need to ensure that the Power BI service can connect to the database and refresh the dataset. Which four actions should you perform, and in what order?

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Configure an on-premises data gateway
  • Step 2: Add a data source
  • Step 3: Add the dataset owner to the data source
  • Step 4: Configure a scheduled refresh
  1. Configure an on-premises data gateway: the cloud service cannot reach an on-premises database without it.
  2. Add a data source to the gateway (server, database and credentials).
  3. Add the dataset owner to the data source so they can use it.
  4. Configure the scheduled refresh (daily) using that gateway.

The virtual network data gateway is for sources inside an Azure VNet, not on-premises SQL Server.

  • Official documentation: What is an on-premises data gateway? - Microsoft Learn | Add or remove a gateway data source - Microsoft Learn | Configure scheduled refresh - Microsoft Learn

links.t: What is an on-premises data gateway?
Add or remove a gateway data source

q018.stem:
You attempt to connect Power BI Desktop to a Cassandra database. From the Get Data connector list, there is no specific connector for Cassandra.

You need to select an alternate data connector. Which type of connector should you choose?
options: Microsoft SQL Server database
ODBC
OLEDB
OData

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: ODBC

Why it is correct: when there is no native connector, the ODBC connector lets you use the database’s ODBC driver (Cassandra has them) installed on the machine.

  • Official documentation: ODBC - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Microsoft SQL Server database — Why it is incorrect: the SQL Server connector speaks only the SQL Server protocol.
  • Option C — OLEDB — Why it is incorrect: OLE DB requires an OLE DB provider for the source; for Cassandra ODBC is the common, available option. Official documentation: OLE DB - Microsoft Learn
  • Option D — OData — Why it is incorrect: OData consumes OData web services, not a Cassandra database. Official documentation: OData feed - Microsoft Learn

q019.stem:
You receive annual sales data to include in Power BI reports. In Power Query Editor you connect to the Excel source shown (columns Month, MonthNumber and one column per year: 2019, 2020 and 2021).

The report must visualize Sales over years and months, add a slicer for the month and add a slicer for the year. Which three actions should you perform, and in what order?

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Select the Month and MonthNumber columns.
  • Step 2: Select Unpivot other columns.
  • Step 3: Rename the Attribute column as Year and the Value column as Sales.
  1. Select Month and MonthNumber: these must stay fixed.
  2. Unpivot other columns: turns all remaining columns (the years) into rows, with Attribute (year) and Value (amount) columns, and also copes with new years being added.
  3. Rename Attribute → Year and Value → Sales, giving you a Year column for the slicer and the Sales value.

Selecting the years and unpivoting “selected columns” would also work, but the offered option is “other columns”. Transpose rotates the whole table and does not apply.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Microsoft Learn

q020.stem:
You use Power BI Desktop to connect to an Azure SQL database with the settings shown: Import mode, no command timeout set and “Navigate using full hierarchy” unchecked.

Complete each statement based on the exhibit. NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The default timeout for the connection from Power BI Desktop to the database will be: 10 minutes
  • The Navigator will display: only tables that contain data
  • 10 minutes: if you do not set “Command timeout in minutes”, the SQL Server connector uses the default of 10 minutes.
  • Only tables that contain data (per the source key): with “Navigate using full hierarchy” unchecked, the Navigator shows a flat list of objects instead of the full hierarchy (schemas → objects).

⚠️ Heads-up: the second value is debatable: part of the community says that, with full hierarchy unchecked, the Navigator lists all tables (with or without data) and the full hierarchy only groups them by schema. The source key is “only tables that contain data”. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: SQL Server database connector - Microsoft Learn

q021.stem:
You have the following Azure SQL databases: db-powerbi-dev (dev.database.windows.net), db-powerbi-uat (uat.database.windows.net) and db-powerbi-prod (prod.database.windows.net).

You plan to build a single PBIX file that must: consume data from the database for each lifecycle stage; NOT use deployment pipelines; minimize administrative effort. What should you do? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Create: One parameter
  • Parameter type: Text
  • One parameter: a single parameter (e.g. the server name) used in the queries’ connection string; you only change its value per stage (in the service, under the model’s parameter settings).
  • Text: the server name is a string. True/False or decimal number cannot hold a server address.

Several parameters would duplicate maintenance for no reason.

  • Official documentation: Query parameters - Microsoft Learn | Parameters in the Power BI service - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Parameters in the Power BI service

q022.stem:
You are creating a query to be used as a Country dimension in a star schema. A snapshot of the source data has Country and City columns (USA/New York, USA/Denver, UK/Manchester, Brazil/Rio, Brazil/São Paulo…).

The dimension must contain a list of unique countries. Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
options: Delete the Country column.
Remove duplicates from the table.
Remove duplicates from the City column.
Delete the City column.
Remove duplicates from the Country column.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option D: Delete the City column.
  • Option E: Remove duplicates from the Country column.

Why it is correct: City is deleted (it does not belong in a country dimension) and duplicates are removed from Country, leaving one row per country. Without both steps you would not have a unique country list with a unique key for relationships.

  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI - Microsoft Learn | Remove duplicates - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Delete the Country column. — Why it is incorrect: you would delete the very column you need.
  • Option B — Remove duplicates from the table. — Why it is incorrect: removing duplicates from the whole table (Country+City) keeps repeated countries, since every city differs.
  • Option C — Remove duplicates from the City column. — Why it is incorrect: deduplicating City does not produce a unique list of countries.

links.t: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

q023.stem:
You use Power Query Editor to preview the sample data: a price column (100, 150, 130…) and a discount column with many Error values (63%).

You need to clean and transform the query so that all rows are kept and error values in the discount column are replaced with 0.05. Minimize administrative effort. Which three actions should you perform, and in what order?

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Select the discount column.
  • Step 2: Select Replace Errors to replace each error value with 0.05.
  • Step 3: For the discount column, change Data Type to Decimal Number.
  1. Select the discount column (the operation applies to the selected column).
  2. Replace Errors with 0.05 keeps every row, unlike Remove Errors.
  3. Change the type to Decimal Number: discounts like 0.05 are decimals; Whole Number would truncate them.

The price column is not selected because it has no errors.

⚠️ Heads-up: the order of steps 2 and 3 is debated: part of the community would change the type to decimal first (many errors come from the wrong type) and then replace the remaining errors. The source key order is shown. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Replace values and errors - Microsoft Learn | Data types in Power Query - Microsoft Learn

q024.stem:
You attempt to use Power Query Editor to create a custom column and receive the error shown in the exhibit (the formula tries to combine a text value and a number).

Complete each statement based on the exhibit. NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The error is caused by: mismatched data types
  • The desired outcome of the custom column is: A1
  • Mismatched data types: the & operator concatenates text; if one operand is a number (1) and the other text (“A”), Power Query returns the type error (“cannot apply operator & to types Text and Number”).
  • A1: the intended result is “A” followed by 1; achieved by converting the number to text (Text.From) before concatenating.
  • Official documentation: Text.From - Microsoft Learn | Add a custom column - Microsoft Learn

q025.stem:
From Power Query Editor, you execute a query and receive the error: Datasource.Error: Could not find file.

What are two possible causes of the error? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
options: You do not have permissions to the file.
An incorrect privacy level was used for the data source.
The file is locked.
The referenced file was moved to a new location.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: You do not have permissions to the file.
  • Option D: The referenced file was moved to a new location.

Why it is correct: “Could not find file” appears when the path no longer points to an accessible file: either it was moved/renamed, or you lack permission to see it (the system answers as if it does not exist).

  • Official documentation: Excel connector - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — An incorrect privacy level was used for the data source. — Why it is incorrect: an incorrect privacy level triggers “Formula.Firewall” errors (combining sources), not file-not-found. Official documentation: Privacy levels - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — The file is locked. — Why it is incorrect: a locked file produces an access/sharing error, not “could not find file”.

q026.stem:
You have data in an Excel worksheet with columns SKU, price and discount; some discount cells contain errors (#REF!).

You need to use Power Query to clean and transform the dataset so that: if the discount column returns an error, 0.05 is used; all rows are kept; administrative effort is minimized. What should you do in Power Query Editor?
options: Select Replace Errors.
Edit the query in the Query Errors group.
Select Remove Errors.
Select Keep Errors.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Select Replace Errors.

Why it is correct: Replace Errors substitutes every error value with the given value (0.05) and keeps all rows, in a single step.

  • Official documentation: Replace values and errors - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — Edit the query in the Query Errors group. — Why it is incorrect: there is no “Query Errors” group that fixes values this way.
  • Option C — Select Remove Errors. — Why it is incorrect: Remove Errors deletes the rows with errors, violating “keep all rows”.
  • Option D — Select Keep Errors. — Why it is incorrect: Keep Errors keeps only the rows with errors and discards the rest.

q027.stem:
You have a CSV file with user complaints. The Logged column contains date and time in the format 2018-12-31 at 08:59.

You need to analyze the complaints by logged date and use a built-in date hierarchy. What should you do?
options: Apply the Parse function from the Data transformations options to the Logged column.
Change the data type of the Logged column to Date.
Split the Logged column by using at as the delimiter.
Create a column by example that starts with 2018-12-31.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Split the Logged column by using at as the delimiter.

Why it is correct: splitting on “at” separates date and time; the date column becomes Date type and enables the date hierarchy.

⚠️ Heads-up: community votes are spread (C majority, but also D and B). The source key is C. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Split columns by delimiter - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Apply the Parse function from the Data transformations options to the Logged column. — Why it is incorrect: Parse cannot interpret text with the word “at” in the middle as a date/time.
  • Option B — Change the data type of the Logged column to Date. — Why it is incorrect: the full value is not a valid date format; the type change would error.
  • Option D — Create a column by example that starts with 2018-12-31. — Why it is incorrect: a column-from-example with a single example is unreliable and not the standard method; splitting by delimiter is deterministic.

q028.stem:
You have two Excel workbooks in a OneDrive folder; each contains a table named Sales with the same structure.

You plan to use Power BI to combine both Sales tables into one and create visuals from it. The solution must let you publish a separate report and dataset.

Which storage mode do you use for the report file and for the dataset file? (Modes: DirectQuery, Import, LiveConnect, Push.) NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Report file: LiveConnect
  • Dataset file: Import
  • Dataset file → Import: the model combines the two Excel tables and caches them; Excel workbooks do not support DirectQuery.
  • Report file → LiveConnect: the report is separated from the model and connects live to the published semantic model, holding no data of its own.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source image says Report: Import / Dataset: DirectQuery, which is impossible with Excel sources (no DirectQuery support). The community proposes Report: LiveConnect / Dataset: Import (separating report and model), which is what is marked here. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Separate reports from models - Microsoft Learn | Storage mode in Power BI Desktop - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Storage mode in Power BI Desktop

q029.stem:
You use Power Query to import two tables named Order Header and Order Details from an Azure SQL database. Order Header relates to Order Details by a column named Order ID in each table.

You need to combine the tables into a single query that contains the unique columns of each table. What should you select in Power Query Editor?
options: Merge queries
Combine files
Append queries

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Merge queries

Why it is correct: Merge queries adds the columns of one table to the other matching on Order ID, so the result contains the unique columns of both.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — Combine files — Why it is incorrect: Combine files unifies several files with the same structure; these tables come from a database. Official documentation: Combine files overview - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — Append queries — Why it is incorrect: Append stacks rows of tables with the same columns; it does not add columns from two different tables. Official documentation: Append queries - Microsoft Learn

q030.stem:
You have a PBIX file that imports data from an Excel source stored in a file share on a local network. You are notified that the Excel source was moved to a new location.

You need to update the PBIX file to use the new location. What are three ways to achieve this? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
options: From the Datasets settings of the Power BI service, configure the data source credentials.
From the Data source settings in Power BI Desktop, configure the file path.
From Current File in Power BI Desktop, configure the Data Load settings.
From Power Query Editor, use the formula bar to configure the file path for the applied step.
From Advanced Editor in Power Query Editor, configure the file path in the M code.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option B: From the Data source settings in Power BI Desktop, configure the file path.
  • Option D: From Power Query Editor, use the formula bar to configure the file path for the applied step.
  • Option E: From Advanced Editor in Power Query Editor, configure the file path in the M code.

Why it is correct: the file path is stored in the PBIX: it can be changed in Data source settings (Change Source), in the Source step formula via the formula bar, or in the M code in the Advanced Editor. All three edit the same query definition.

  • Official documentation: Data sources in Power BI Desktop - Microsoft Learn | Power Query user interface - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — From the Datasets settings of the Power BI service, configure the data source credentials. — Why it is incorrect: data source credentials do not change the PBIX file path. Official documentation: Manage data sources - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — From Current File in Power BI Desktop, configure the Data Load settings. — Why it is incorrect: the current file’s Data Load settings (cache, types…) do not include the source path.

links.t: Data sources in Power BI Desktop

q031.stem:
You have a folder that contains 50 JSON files. You need to use Power BI Desktop to make the metadata of the files available as a single dataset. The solution must NOT store the data of the JSON files.

Which type of data source should you use, and which transformation should you perform? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Data source type: Folder
  • Transformation: Delete the Content column.
  • Folder: returns one row per file with its metadata (name, extension, dates, path) and the Content column with the binary. The JSON or Text/CSV connectors open a single file.
  • Delete the Content column: Content holds the JSON data; removing it meets the “do not store the data” requirement and leaves the metadata.

Combining Content would load the data; deleting Attributes would remove metadata.

⚠️ Heads-up: some users note that Attributes should also be expanded to see all metadata; the source key only marks deleting Content. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Folder connector - Microsoft Learn

q032.stem:
Northwind Traders case study (food import company): sources Source1 (Azure SQL Database with Orders, Products, Suppliers, Categories, Order Details and Sales Employees) and Source2 (Excel exported daily to SharePoint Online with Customer Details). Technical requirements: a single model for all three reports, data current as of 7 AM Pacific each day, fast response times and minimum model size. RLS applies only to the sales department with [EmailAddress] = USERNAME() on Sales Employees.

You need to create the semantic model. Which storage mode should you use for the tables?
options: DirectQuery
Dual
Import
Live connection

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Import

Why it is correct: data only needs to be current once a day (7 AM) with fast responses and a compact model: Import caches compressed data in memory, is fastest and refreshes on a daily schedule. Also Source2 (Excel) supports Import only.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source key marks B (Dual) while most of the community votes C (Import); C is marked here, which fits the requirements (daily refresh, performance, size). Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Storage mode in Power BI Desktop - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — DirectQuery — Why it is incorrect: DirectQuery is slower on every interaction and unnecessary because real time is not required; Excel does not support it. Official documentation: DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn
  • Option B — Dual — Why it is incorrect: Dual only makes sense in composite models with DirectQuery tables; there are none here.
  • Option D — Live connection — Why it is incorrect: live connection uses an already published model; here the model must be built from the sources.

links.t: Storage mode in Power BI Desktop

q033.stem:
You have a Power BI semantic model with these data sources: Employee review data (contains sensitive information; must NOT be folded into any other data source) and Sales opportunities (less sensitive; must only be available internally).

You need to configure the privacy level of each source. NOTE: each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Employee review data: Private
  • Sales opportunities: Organizational
  • Employee review data → Private: private sources hold sensitive or confidential data and are never sent to other sources (no folding), exactly what is required.
  • Sales opportunities → Organizational: organizational data can be shared with other organizational sources in the company but not with public sources; it fits “internal only”.

None ignores privacy and Public is for data open to anyone.

  • Official documentation: Privacy levels (Power Query) - Microsoft Learn

q034.stem: You plan to use Power BI Desktop to create a bug-tracking dashboard that pulls data from Analytics in Azure DevOps. You must configure a connector that authenticates to Azure DevOps and: uses Analytics views and filters data from the cloud. Which connector should you use?
options: OData queries
Azure DevOps (Boards only)
Azure DevOps Server (Boards only)
OData Feed

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: OData Feed

Why it is correct: the OData Feed connector queries the cloud Analytics OData service with the organization URL and lets you filter at the source (OData query); it is the option the source marks for this scenario.

⚠️ Heads-up: the community is split (D 13, B 9, A 8 votes) and the current documentation recommends the “Azure DevOps (Boards only)” connector for Analytics views. D, the source key, is kept. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Connect with Power BI Data Connector / OData - Microsoft Learn | OData feed - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — OData queries — Why it is incorrect: “OData queries” is not a Power BI Desktop connector; OData queries are written inside the OData Feed connector.
  • Option B — Azure DevOps (Boards only) — Why it is incorrect: the Azure DevOps (Boards only) connector returns Boards data with a predefined model and does not let you pick Analytics views or custom OData filters.
  • Option C — Azure DevOps Server (Boards only) — Why it is incorrect: Azure DevOps Server is the on-premises edition; the requirement is cloud data.

links.t: Connect with Power BI Data Connector / OData

q035.stem:
You use Power Query Editor to preview the data shown: the first two rows contain title text and the column names are in row 3.

You confirm that the data will always start on row 3 and that row 3 will always contain the column names. How should you shape the query? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • To configure the query to start on row 3, select: Remove top rows
  • To use the values in row 3 as the column names, select: Use first row as headers
  • Remove top rows (2 rows): discards the title rows so row 3 becomes first. Keep top rows would do the opposite.
  • Use first row as headers: promotes the new first row (old row 3) to headers.
  • Official documentation: Promote or demote column headers - Microsoft Learn | Remove top rows - Microsoft Learn

q036.stem:
Note: this question is part of a series that presents the same scenario; each question has a unique solution and several, or none, may be valid.

You have a data source with a column that contains case-sensitive data. You have a Power BI semantic model in DirectQuery mode. You connect to the model and discover that it contains undefined values and errors. You need to resolve the issue.

Solution: You implicitly convert the values into the required type.

Does this meet the goal?
options: Yes
No

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: the cause is case differences between the source (case-sensitive) and the model (case-insensitive); an implicit type conversion does not normalize them.

  • Official documentation: DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn | DirectQuery data sources - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Yes — Why it is incorrect: an implicit conversion does not fix case sensitivity and the undefined values persist.

q037.stem:
Note: this question is part of a series that presents the same scenario; each question has a unique solution and several, or none, may be valid.

You have a data source with a column that contains case-sensitive data. You have a Power BI semantic model in DirectQuery mode. You connect to the model and discover that it contains undefined values and errors. You need to resolve the issue.

Solution: You change the semantic model mode.

Does this meet the goal?
options: Yes
No

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: No

Why it is correct: changing the mode (e.g. to Import) is not the root fix: the case inconsistency is in the data and would still have to be normalized; it also alters the refresh requirements.

⚠️ Heads-up: there is little community input (2 votes for B); this is a series question with an unofficial solution. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn | DirectQuery data sources - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Yes — Why it is incorrect: changing the mode does not solve data normalization.

q038.stem:
Note: this question is part of a series that presents the same scenario; each question has a unique solution and several, or none, may be valid.

You have a data source with a column that contains case-sensitive data. You have a Power BI semantic model in DirectQuery mode. You connect to the model and discover that it contains undefined values and errors. You need to resolve the issue.

Solution: You normalize casing in the source query or Power Query Editor.

Does this meet the goal?
options: Yes
No

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Yes

Why it is correct: normalizing casing (e.g. UPPER or Text.Upper) in the source query or in Power Query makes the values match and removes the undefined values and errors caused by that difference.

⚠️ Heads-up: in DirectQuery mode, normalizing in Power Query only works if the transformation folds to the source; the community votes A (4) vs B (1). Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Text.Upper - Microsoft Learn | DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn | DirectQuery data sources - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — No — Why it is incorrect: it does meet the goal, see “Why it is correct”.

q039.stem:
Note: this question is part of a series that presents the same scenario; each question has a unique solution and several, or none, may be valid.

You have a data source with a column that contains case-sensitive data. You have a Power BI semantic model in DirectQuery mode. You connect to the model and discover that it contains undefined values and errors. You need to resolve the issue.

Solution: You add an index key and normalize casing in the data source.

Does this meet the goal?
options: Yes
No

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Yes

Why it is correct: normalizing casing in the data source removes the cause; the index key guarantees row uniqueness and avoids undefined values from ambiguous keys.

⚠️ Heads-up: the community is split (A 4, B 3); the source key is A. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn | DirectQuery data sources - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — No — Why it is incorrect: it does meet the goal.

q040.stem:
You have an Excel file in a OneDrive folder that must be imported to a Power BI semantic model. You need to ensure the model can be refreshed in powerbi.com.

Which two connectors can you use? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
options: Web
Excel Workbook
Folder
Text/CSV
SharePoint folder

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: Web
  • Option E: SharePoint folder

Why it is correct: to refresh in the service without a gateway the file must be reachable by cloud URL: the Web connector (with the file link) or SharePoint folder (OneDrive for Business sits on SharePoint).

⚠️ Heads-up: the community votes BE (6) vs AE (4); as in the equivalent T1-11, the source key AE is kept. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: SharePoint folder - Microsoft Learn | Use OneDrive for Business links in Power BI Desktop - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — Excel Workbook — Why it is incorrect: with the local OneDrive path it needs a gateway to refresh in the service.
  • Option C — Folder — Why it is incorrect: Folder is for local/network file systems: it requires a gateway.
  • Option D — Text/CSV — Why it is incorrect: Text/CSV does not match the file format (Excel) and with a local path also needs a gateway.

links.t: Use OneDrive for Business links in Power BI Desktop

q041.stem:
You use Power Query Editor to preview a column named Date with values like 01-01-2014 (16 distinct, 0 unique).

You need to change the Date column to contain only the year. The solution must minimize administrative effort. What should you do?
options: Split the column by delimiter.
Split the column by number of characters.
Extract the text after the delimiter.
Transform the column to contain only the year.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Transform the column to contain only the year.

Why it is correct: the column is of date type, so the Date → Year transformation converts it directly into the year in one step, independent of text format.

  • Official documentation: Transform columns (date/time) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Split the column by delimiter. — Why it is incorrect: splitting leaves several columns and extra steps to discard the rest. Official documentation: Split columns by delimiter - Microsoft Learn
  • Option B — Split the column by number of characters. — Why it is incorrect: it depends on the exact character count and is fragile.
  • Option C — Extract the text after the delimiter. — Why it is incorrect: extracting text after the delimiter works on text and would return “mm-yyyy”, not just the year.

q042.stem:
You are designing the data model for a Power BI semantic model. You have these star-schema tables: Date (one row per day; Date identifies the row), Patient (one row per patient; Patient key identifies the row), Test (one row per test; Test key identifies the row) and Test Result (one row per administered test with date, test key, patient key, result value and comments).

Which table is the fact table, and which column is a surrogate key? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Fact table: Test Result
  • Surrogate key: Patient key
  • Test Result: it holds the measurable value (result) and the foreign keys to Date, Test and Patient: it is the fact table. The others are dimensions.
  • Patient key: it is the unique identifier generated for the model, independent of the source system (which provides Patient source ID). Date of birth and last name are not unique.
  • Official documentation: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

q043.stem:
You use Power BI Desktop to import two tables, Customer (Customer_Name, Customer ID, Website) and Contacts (Contact ID, Contact Email, Contact Name, Customer Name). A web-based contact form fills the Contacts table and the data is not sanitized.

You need to create a merge for the Customer and Contacts tables. What should you do?
options: Disable fuzzy matching.
Enable fuzzy matching.
Set Join Kind to Left Outer.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Enable fuzzy matching.

Why it is correct: matching is on customer names typed in a form (typos, casing, spaces); fuzzy matching joins similar values, not only identical ones.

  • Official documentation: Fuzzy matching - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Disable fuzzy matching. — Why it is incorrect: exact matching would fail with misspelled names or formatting differences.
  • Option C — Set Join Kind to Left Outer. — Why it is incorrect: the join kind decides which rows are kept, not whether dirty keys match. Official documentation: Left outer join - Microsoft Learn

q044.stem:
You are using Power BI Desktop to profile data in Power Query Editor. The table shows a date column (text, “2024-02-07”) and a data.Entries.menuAmount column with values 01/01/1900, 02/01/1900 and an Error.

Complete each statement based on the exhibit. NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Before you can transform the date column to show only the day, you must: use the Parse command on the column.
  • To fix the error displayed for the data.Entries.menuAmount column, you must: change the data type.
  • Parse: the date column is text; the Parse command interprets the text as a date so the day can then be extracted.
  • Change the data type: the error arises because the menuAmount type does not match the values; fixing the type removes the error. Renaming or conditional formatting does not affect the data.

⚠️ Heads-up: the community notes that in both cases you would change the data type first; the source key marks Parse for the first one. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Data types in Power Query - Microsoft Learn | Transform columns (date/time) - Microsoft Learn

q045.stem:
You have a Power BI semantic model named Model1 with a Sales table of 10 million records: PurchaseID (text, unique order ID), CustomerID (text, unique customer ID), PurchaseDateTime (date/time/timezone), Region (text) and TotalAmount (decimal).

The related report shows weekly sales by region. You need to minimize the size of Model1. How should you modify the CustomerID and PurchaseDateTime columns? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • CustomerID: Remove the column.
  • PurchaseDateTime: Split the column into separate date and time columns.
  • CustomerID → remove the column: it is a unique identifier with 10 million distinct values (maximum cardinality) and the weekly-sales-by-region report does not use it; it takes the most space.
  • PurchaseDateTime → split into date and time: a date-time column has very high cardinality; split, the date has few values and the time can be dropped or reduced, compressing far better.

Changing to Binary/Duration does not reduce cardinality, and removing duplicates on a unique ID changes nothing.

  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling

q046.stem:
You have a Power BI Desktop report named Report1 that uses an Azure SQL database as a data source. A user named User1 plans to create a report by using the same data source as Report1.

You need to simplify the connection to the data source for User1. Which type of file should you create?
options: PBIDS
XLSX
PBIT
PBIX

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: PBIDS

Why it is correct: a PBIDS (Power BI data source) file stores only the connection settings (server, database…); on opening it Power BI Desktop asks for credentials and takes the user straight to getting data from the same source.

  • Official documentation: Power BI data source (PBIDS) files - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — XLSX — Why it is incorrect: XLSX is an Excel workbook, not a Power BI connection format.
  • Option C — PBIT — Why it is incorrect: PBIT is a template with model, queries and visuals; more than needed and not just a connection shortcut. Official documentation: Power BI Desktop templates - Microsoft Learn
  • Option D — PBIX — Why it is incorrect: PBIX holds the full report and model; it is not a simple connection shortcut.

q047.stem:
You have a Power BI semantic model that contains values that display as errors. You need to use data profiling features in Power Query to preview the data and identify the issues.

What should you select to gain insight into the number of errors and what should you select to resolve them? NOTE: each correct answer is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • To gain insight, select: Column quality
  • To resolve the errors, select: Replace Errors
  • Column quality: shows the percentage of valid, error and empty values per column.
  • Replace Errors: replaces errors with a valid value without losing rows. Column distribution shows value frequency, not errors.
  • Official documentation: Data profiling tools - Microsoft Learn | Replace values and errors - Microsoft Learn

q048.stem:
You plan to create a Power BI semantic model named Model1 that will contain data from an Azure SQL database named DB1. Model1 must show updated data within two minutes of the data being updated in DB1.

You need to select a connectivity mode for the connection to DB1. What should you choose?
options: DirectQuery
Live connection
Import

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: DirectQuery

Why it is correct: DirectQuery queries DB1 on every interaction, so changes appear almost immediately, without relying on a scheduled refresh.

  • Official documentation: DirectQuery in Power BI - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — Live connection — Why it is incorrect: live connection is for Analysis Services/published models, not for a SQL database.
  • Option C — Import — Why it is incorrect: Import refreshes on schedule (at most 8/day on Pro / 48 on Premium), with no two-minute guarantee. Official documentation: Data refresh in Power BI - Microsoft Learn

q049.stem:
You need to create a semantic model in Power BI Desktop that meets: the model contains an Orders table with one row per order and each row has the total order amount; orders must be filtered by the CustomerID value; users must select the CustomerID value from a list; the list of customers must come from an OData source.

Which three objects should you create in Power Query Editor? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
options: An Orders query that has a filter on CustomerID.
A Customers query that has a filter on CustomerID.
An Orders query that has a single column containing a list of customers.
A Customers query that has a single column containing a list of customer IDs.
A parameter for CustomerID that uses a query to populate the suggested values.
A parameter for CustomerID that uses manually entered values to populate the suggested values.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: An Orders query that has a filter on CustomerID.
  • Option D: A Customers query that has a single column containing a list of customer IDs.
  • Option E: A parameter for CustomerID that uses a query to populate the suggested values.

Why it is correct: three pieces are needed: (1) a single-column Customers query of CustomerID values from the OData source; (2) a CustomerID parameter whose suggested values come from that query (dropdown list); (3) the Orders query filtered by the parameter value.

  • Official documentation: Query parameters - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — A Customers query that has a filter on CustomerID. — Why it is incorrect: filtering Customers by CustomerID does not create the selection list; the list must be a column of IDs.
  • Option C — An Orders query that has a single column containing a list of customers. — Why it is incorrect: the customer list must come from Customers (OData), not Orders.
  • Option F — A parameter for CustomerID that uses manually entered values to populate the suggested values. — Why it is incorrect: manually entered values do not come from the OData source and do not stay current.

q050.stem:
You are creating a report in Power BI Desktop. You load a data extract that includes a free-text field named col1.

You need to analyze the frequency distribution of the string lengths in col1. The solution must not affect the size of the model. What should you do?
options: In the report, add a DAX calculated column that calculates the length of col1.
In the report, add a DAX function that calculates the average length of col1.
From Power Query Editor, add a column that calculates the length of col1.
From Power Query Editor, change the distribution for the Column profile to group by length for col1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: From Power Query Editor, change the distribution for the Column profile to group by length for col1.

Why it is correct: the Column profile in Power Query lets you group the distribution by text length: you get the length histogram purely for analysis, without adding columns to the model, so its size does not change.

  • Official documentation: Data profiling tools - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — In the report, add a DAX calculated column that calculates the length of col1. — Why it is incorrect: a calculated column is stored in the model and increases its size.
  • Option B — In the report, add a DAX function that calculates the average length of col1. — Why it is incorrect: an average is a single summary value, not a frequency distribution.
  • Option C — From Power Query Editor, add a column that calculates the length of col1. — Why it is incorrect: adding a column in Power Query loads it into the model and also increases its size.

q051.stem:
You have a collection of reports for the HR department. The datasets use row-level security (RLS). The company has multiple sales regions, each with an HR manager.

You need to ensure the HR managers can interact with the data from their region only and cannot change the layout of the reports. How should you provision access?
options: Publish the reports in an app and grant the HR managers access permission.
Create a new workspace, copy the datasets and reports, and add the HR managers as members of the workspace.
Publish the reports to a different workspace other than the one hosting the datasets.
Add the HR managers as members of the existing workspace that hosts the reports and the datasets.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Publish the reports in an app and grant the HR managers access permission.

Why it is correct: app users are consumers: they can view and interact with reports but not edit their layout, and RLS applies to them.

  • Official documentation: Publish an app - Microsoft Learn | Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — Create a new workspace, copy the datasets and reports, and add the HR managers as members of the workspace. — Why it is incorrect: as workspace members they could edit content, and RLS is not effectively enforced for roles with edit permissions. Official documentation: Roles in workspaces - Microsoft Learn
  • Option C — Publish the reports to a different workspace other than the one hosting the datasets. — Why it is incorrect: using a different workspace does not stop whoever holds an edit role from changing the report.
  • Option D — Add the HR managers as members of the existing workspace that hosts the reports and the datasets. — Why it is incorrect: members can edit and bypass RLS.

q052.stem: You need to give a user the ability to add members to a workspace, using the principle of least privilege. Which role should you assign?
options: Viewer
Admin
Contributor
Member

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Member

Why it is correct: the Member role can add other people with the Member role or lower (Contributor, Viewer) without the full administrative privileges of Admin.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Viewer — Why it is incorrect: Viewer can only read content.
  • Option B — Admin — Why it is incorrect: Admin can also add members but has more privileges than needed (delete the workspace, manage admins…); it violates least privilege.
  • Option C — Contributor — Why it is incorrect: Contributor can create and edit content but cannot add people.

q053.stem:
You build a report to analyze customer transactions from a database with the tables Customer (CustomerID, primary key) and Transaction (TransactionID, primary key; CustomerID, foreign key).

You import the tables. Which relationship should you use to link them?
options: One-to-many from Transaction to Customer
One-to-one between Customer and Transaction
Many-to-many between Customer and Transaction
One-to-many from Customer to Transaction

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: One-to-many from Customer to Transaction

Why it is correct: one customer (primary key, “one” side) can have many transactions (foreign key, “many” side): one-to-many from Customer to Transaction.

  • Official documentation: Create and manage relationships - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — One-to-many from Transaction to Customer — Why it is incorrect: it reverses the sides: the “one” side must be the table with the unique key (Customer).
  • Option B — One-to-one between Customer and Transaction — Why it is incorrect: one-to-one would require each customer to have at most one transaction.
  • Option C — Many-to-many between Customer and Transaction — Why it is incorrect: many-to-many is not needed when one of the columns is a unique key.

q054.stem:
You have a custom connector that returns ID, From, To, Subject, Body and Has Attachments for every email sent during the past year (more than 10 million records).

You build a report analyzing employees’ internal networks based on whom they email. You must prevent report recipients from reading the analyzed emails while minimizing the model size. What should you do?
options: From Model view, set the Subject and Body columns to Hidden.
Remove the Subject and Body columns during the import.
Implement row-level security (RLS) so that the report recipients can only see results based on the emails they sent.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Remove the Subject and Body columns during the import.

Why it is correct: if the columns are not imported, the content never reaches the model: nobody can read it and the size drops (Body is the heaviest column). Network analysis only needs From/To.

  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — From Model view, set the Subject and Body columns to Hidden. — Why it is incorrect: hiding only conceals them in report view; they stay in the model (using space) and remain reachable, e.g. via Analyze in Excel or XMLA.
  • Option C — Implement row-level security (RLS) so that the report recipients can only see results based on the emails they sent. — Why it is incorrect: RLS filters rows, does not hide columns, and does not reduce model size. Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling

q055.stem:
You have a custom connector that returns ID, From, To, Subject, Body and Has Attachments for every email sent during the past year (more than 10 million records).

You build a report analyzing employees’ internal networks based on whom they email. You must prevent report recipients from reading the analyzed emails while minimizing the model size. What should you do?
options: From Model view, set the Subject and Body columns to Hidden.
Remove the Subject and Body columns during the import.
Implement row-level security (RLS) so that the report recipients can only see results based on the emails they sent.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Remove the Subject and Body columns during the import.

Why it is correct: if the columns are not imported, the content never reaches the model: nobody can read it and the size drops (Body is the heaviest column). Network analysis only needs From/To.

  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — From Model view, set the Subject and Body columns to Hidden. — Why it is incorrect: hiding only conceals them in report view; they stay in the model and remain reachable by other means.
  • Option C — Implement row-level security (RLS) so that the report recipients can only see results based on the emails they sent. — Why it is incorrect: RLS filters rows, does not hide columns, and does not reduce model size. Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling

q056.stem: You create a Power BI dataset that contains the table shown in the exhibit (Business Unit: Cost Center, Headcount, ID, Name). You need to make the table available as an organizational data type in Microsoft Excel. How should you configure the table properties? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Row label: Cost Center
  • Key column: ID
  • Is featured table: Yes
  • Row label → Cost Center: the value Excel shows in the linked cell and in the information card to identify the row.
  • Key column → ID: provides the unique ID per row so Excel can link a cell to a specific row.
  • Is featured table → Yes: only featured tables appear in Excel’s Data Types Gallery for the organization.
  • Official documentation: Set up featured tables for Excel - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Set up featured tables for Excel

q057.stem:
You have the Power BI model shown (Country, Calendar, Purchase, Purchase Detail). A manager can represent only a single country.

You need to use RLS so each manager sees only the data of their country, and minimize the number of RLS roles. Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
options: Create a single role that filters Country[Manager Email] by using the USERNAME DAX function.
Create a single role that filters Country[Manager_Email] by using the USEROBJECTID DAX function.
For the relationship between Purchase Detail and Purchase, select Apply security filter in both directions.
Create one role for each country.
For the relationship between Purchase and Purchase Detail, change the Cross filter direction to Single.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: Create a single role that filters Country[Manager Email] by using the USERNAME DAX function.
  • Option C: For the relationship between Purchase Detail and Purchase, select Apply security filter in both directions.

Why it is correct: one dynamic role with [Manager Email] = USERNAME() serves every manager (minimum roles). The security filter must also propagate from Purchase to Purchase Detail; with the bidirectional relationship and “Apply security filter in both directions” the country filter reaches the detail table.

⚠️ Heads-up: the community is split (AC 7 votes, AD 3, AB 2); AC, the source key, is kept. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn | Row-level security guidance - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — Create a single role that filters Country[Manager_Email] by using the USEROBJECTID DAX function. — Why it is incorrect: USEROBJECTID is not a DAX function for RLS; the functions are USERNAME and USERPRINCIPALNAME.
  • Option D — Create one role for each country. — Why it is incorrect: one role per country is the opposite of minimizing roles.
  • Option E — For the relationship between Purchase and Purchase Detail, change the Cross filter direction to Single. — Why it is incorrect: a single direction would not carry the filter through the chain as required, and it is not what is asked.

q058.stem:
You have an imported Power BI dataset with the data model shown (Employee and dimensions: Ethnicity, SeparationReason, Date, FP, PayType, Gender, BU, AgeGroup).

Select the choice that completes each statement based on the graphic. NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Changing the [?] setting of the relationships will improve report query performance: Assume Referential Integrity
  • The data model is organized into a [?]: star schema
  • Assume Referential Integrity: makes queries use inner joins instead of outer joins, which are more efficient. It requires the “many”-side column to have no nulls or unmatched values.
  • Star schema: a central fact table (Employee) surrounded by dimension tables with no further normalization levels.

⚠️ Heads-up: “Assume referential integrity” is only available with DirectQuery, yet the statement speaks of an imported dataset; the source key marks it anyway. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Assume referential integrity - Microsoft Learn | Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Understand star schema and the importance for Power BI

q059.stem:
You have a Power BI model with a Sales table (with a measure named Total Sales) and a related date table. You need to create a measure that calculates the total sales from the equivalent month of the previous year.

How should you complete the calculation? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Sales Previous Year = [?] ( [Total Sales], …: CALCULATE
  • Time function: PARALLELPERIOD
  • Dates column: 'Date'[Date]
  • CALCULATE: modifies the filter context to evaluate [Total Sales] over another period.
  • PARALLELPERIOD: returns a parallel period shifted by a number of intervals (e.g. -12 months); it is the source-key option. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR would return last year’s dates, not the interval shift this template offers; DATESMTD and TOTALMTD are “month to date”.
  • 'Date'[Date]: the function needs a contiguous date column with no gaps.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source key marks 'Date'[Month] for the third dropdown, but PARALLELPERIOD requires a date column ('Date'[Date]); the latter is marked here. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: PARALLELPERIOD (DAX) - Microsoft Learn | SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR (DAX) - Microsoft Learn

q060.stem:
You plan to create a report that will display sales data from the last year for multiple regions. You need to restrict access to individual rows of data on a per-region basis by using roles.

Which four actions should you perform, and in what order?

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Import the data to Power BI Desktop.
  • Step 2: Create a role definition.
  • Step 3: Assign users to the role.
  • Step 4: Publish the report.
  1. Import the data into Power BI Desktop.
  2. Create the role definition (Modeling → Manage roles → region filter DAX).
  3. Assign users to the role: done in the Power BI service, not in Desktop.
  4. Publish the report (this also publishes the role definitions).

“Add a filter to the report” is not security: a report filter can be removed.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source order places “Assign users” before “Publish”; in practice assignment happens in the service once the model is published. The source key order is shown. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn

q061.stem:
You create a data model in Power BI and developers say it is too complex. Tables: Sales_Region (region_id, name), Region_Manager (region_id, manager_id), Sales_Manager (sales_manager_id, name, region_id) and Manager (manager_id, name).

Relationships: one-to-one between Sales_Region and Region_Manager; Sales_Manager has more records than Sales_Region but every Sales_Region record has one in Sales_Manager; Manager has more records than Region_Manager but every Region_Manager record has one in Manager.

You need to denormalize the model into a single table including only managers associated with a sales region. Which three actions should you perform, and in what order? (More than one order is correct.)

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Merge [Sales_Region] and [Sales_Manager] by using an inner join.
  • Step 2: Merge [Region_Manager] and [Manager] by using an inner join.
  • Step 3: Merge [Sales_Region] and [Region_Manager] by using a right join as a new query named [Sales_Region_and_Region_Manager].
  1. Sales_Region + Sales_Manager (inner join): only regions with their sales manager.
  2. Region_Manager + Manager (inner join): every Region_Manager has its Manager; the inner join keeps only matched rows.
  3. Join the results into a new query containing only managers associated with a region.

Only inner joins guarantee “only associated”; outer joins would keep unmatched rows.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source key uses a right join in the third step, which could keep unmatched rows; the community does not clearly challenge it. The source key is shown. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Merge queries overview - Microsoft Learn | Inner join - Microsoft Learn

q062.stem:
You have a Power BI report. The PBIX file is 550 MB and the report is accessed through an app workspace in shared capacity on powerbi.com.

The report uses an imported dataset with a 12-million-row fact table, refreshed twice a day (08:00 and 17:00). It is a single page with 15 AppSource visuals and 10 default visuals.

Users say the report is slow to load visuals. You need to recommend a solution to improve performance. What do you recommend?
options: Change any DAX measures to use iterator functions.
Enable visual interactions.
Replace the default visuals with AppSource visuals.
Split the visuals onto multiple pages.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Split the visuals onto multiple pages.

Why it is correct: each visual issues queries when the page loads; with 25 visuals on one page loading is slow. Spreading them across pages reduces the concurrent queries per page.

  • Official documentation: Optimize report performance - Microsoft Learn | Troubleshoot report performance - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Change any DAX measures to use iterator functions. — Why it is incorrect: iterators are usually more expensive than simple aggregations.
  • Option B — Enable visual interactions. — Why it is incorrect: enabling interactions increases cross-visual work rather than reducing it.
  • Option C — Replace the default visuals with AppSource visuals. — Why it is incorrect: AppSource visuals are usually slower than built-in ones.

q063.stem:
You use an imported Power BI data model to perform basket analysis. The goal is to identify which products are usually bought together in the same transaction and within sales territories.

You import a fact table Sales with columns such as SalesRowID, ProductKey, OrderDateKey (surrogate key in YYYYMMDD format), OrderDate, CustomerKey, SalesTerritoryKey, SalesOrderNumber, SalesOrderLineNumber, OrderQuantity, LineTotal, TaxAmt, Freight, LastModified and AuditID. Related dimension tables are imported.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true; otherwise No.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • The SalesRowID and AuditID columns can be removed from the model without impeding the analysis goals.: Yes
  • Both the OrderDateKey and OrderDate columns are necessary to perform the basket analysis.: No
  • The TaxAmt column must retain the current number of decimal places to perform the basket analysis.: No
  • 1 → Yes: SalesRowID (technical row id) and AuditID (load-process id) add nothing to which-products-are-bought-together analysis; removing them shrinks the model.
  • 2 → No: OrderDateKey (surrogate key) and OrderDate represent the same thing; one is enough (the key to relate to the date dimension).
  • 3 → No: tax is irrelevant to basket analysis; the column is not even needed, let alone its decimal precision.
  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling

q064.stem:
You have a Power BI model with three tables: Orders, Date and City. There is a one-to-many relationship between Date and Orders and between City and Orders.

The model has two RLS roles. Role1 filters City[State Province] = "Kentucky"; Role2 filters Date[Calendar Year] = 2020.

If a user is a member of both roles, what data will they see in a report that uses the model?
options: The user will see data for which the State Province value is Kentucky or where the Calendar Year is 2020.
The user will receive an error and will not be able to see the data in the report.
The user will only see data for which the State Province value is Kentucky.
The user will only see data for which the State Province value is Kentucky and the Calendar Year is 2020.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: The user will see data for which the State Province value is Kentucky or where the Calendar Year is 2020.

Why it is correct: when a user belongs to several RLS roles, the permissions are additive (union): they see whatever any role allows. Here, Kentucky (Role1) or year 2020 (Role2).

⚠️ Heads-up: the community is split (A 31, D 28): D would be right if both filters were in the same role. With two separate roles the documentation indicates a union. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option B — The user will receive an error and will not be able to see the data in the report. — Why it is incorrect: there is no conflict between roles that raises an error; they are simply combined.
  • Option C — The user will only see data for which the State Province value is Kentucky. — Why it is incorrect: it ignores Role2, which also grants access.
  • Option D — The user will only see data for which the State Province value is Kentucky and the Calendar Year is 2020. — Why it is incorrect: that intersection would apply if both filters were in a single role, not in two separate roles.

q065.stem:
Note: this question is part of a series with the same scenario; each has a unique solution.

q068.stem:
You are preparing a financial report in Power BI and connect to an Excel spreadsheet through Power Query Editor: the first row holds Measure, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, with the measures Revenue, Overheads and Cost of Goods below.

You need to prepare the data for visualizations that include all measures over time and year-over-year calculations for all the measures. Which four actions should you perform, and in what order?

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Transpose the table.
  • Step 2: Use the first row as headers.
  • Step 3: Unpivot all the columns other than Measure.
  • Step 4: Rename the Measure column as Year.

Each measure must become a column and each year a row (the right shape for time series and year-over-year calculations):

  1. Transpose the table: measures become columns and years become rows.
  2. Use the first row as headers (the measure names).
  3. Unpivot the columns other than the first, per the source key.
  4. Rename the Measure column as Year.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source key order is debatable: after transposing and promoting headers, the column holding years is named “Measure” and no unpivot of measures is needed; review the sequence against the linked documentation. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: Unpivot columns - Microsoft Learn | Transpose a table - Microsoft Learn

  • Teacher First Name → Teacher fact (per the source key).
  • Period Number → Attendance fact: the analysis counts students by period and day; keeping the period in the attendance fact avoids extra joins and matches the analysis grain.

q071.stem:
You have the Power BI model shown: a Departments table (DepartmentID, DepartmentName) related to ConfidentialData (DepartmentID). There are four departments.

You need to ensure users can see the data of their respective department only. What should you do?
options: Create a slicer that filters Departments based on DepartmentID.
Create a row-level security (RLS) role for each department, and then define the membership of the role.
Create a DepartmentID parameter to filter the Departments table.
To the ConfidentialData table, add a calculated measure that uses the CURRENTGROUP DAX function.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Create a row-level security (RLS) role for each department, and then define the membership of the role.

Why it is correct: RLS restricts rows in the model based on role membership; with one role per department (DepartmentID filter) each user only sees their department and cannot bypass it.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security (RLS) with Power BI - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Create a slicer that filters Departments based on DepartmentID. — Why it is incorrect: a slicer is a user-changeable filter; it is not security.
  • Option C — Create a DepartmentID parameter to filter the Departments table. — Why it is incorrect: a parameter does not restrict what each user can see.
  • Option D — To the ConfidentialData table, add a calculated measure that uses the CURRENTGROUP DAX function. — Why it is incorrect: CURRENTGROUP is a table function for groupings; it implements no security.

q072.stem: In Power BI Desktop you are building a sales report with two tables, both with RLS configured. You need to create a relationship between them and ensure bidirectional cross-filtering honors the RLS settings. What should you do?
options: Create an inactive relationship between the tables and select Apply security filter in both directions.
Create an active relationship between the tables and select Apply security filter in both directions.
Create an inactive relationship between the tables and select Assume referential integrity.
Create an active relationship between the tables and select Assume referential integrity.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: Create an active relationship between the tables and select Apply security filter in both directions.

Why it is correct: “Apply security filter in both directions” makes RLS propagate both ways across a bidirectional relationship, and the relationship must be active for it to filter.

  • Official documentation: Row-level security guidance - Microsoft Learn | Create and manage relationships - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Create an inactive relationship between the tables and select Apply security filter in both directions. — Why it is incorrect: an inactive relationship does not propagate filters unless activated with USERELATIONSHIP.
  • Option C — Create an inactive relationship between the tables and select Assume referential integrity. — Why it is incorrect: inactive, and “referential integrity” is unrelated to security.
  • Option D — Create an active relationship between the tables and select Assume referential integrity. — Why it is incorrect: “Assume referential integrity” only optimizes DirectQuery queries; it does not control RLS propagation. Official documentation: Assume referential integrity - Microsoft Learn

q074.stem:
You have a Power BI report with the tables Balances (daily closing balance records for every active bank account, through the last day it is live) and Date (one record per day, 2000 to 2025). You have the measure: Accounts := CALCULATE( DISTINCTCOUNT( Balances[AccountID] ), LASTDATE( 'Date'[Date] ) ).

For each statement, select Yes if it is true; otherwise No.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • A table visual that displays the date hierarchy at the year level and [Accounts] will show the total number of accounts that were live throughout the year.: No
  • At the month level and [Accounts] will show the total number of accounts that were live throughout the month.: No
  • At the day level and [Accounts] will show the total number of accounts that were live that day.: Yes

LASTDATE reduces the date context to the last day of the current period, so the measure counts distinct accounts only on the last day of the period.

  • Year → No: it counts accounts live on the last day of the year, not throughout the year.
  • Month → No: likewise, only the last day of the month.
  • Day → Yes: the last date of a single day is that day; it returns accounts live that day.
  • Official documentation: LASTDATE (DAX) - Microsoft Learn | DISTINCTCOUNT (DAX) - Microsoft Learn

q075.stem:
You have an Impressions table (about 30 million records per month) with Ad_id, Site_name, Impression_date, related to a campaigns table (campaignID).

You need an ad analytics system that: presents impression counts by day, campaign and site_name; covers the last year; and minimizes the model size. Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
options: Create one-to-many relationships between the tables.
Group the Impressions query in Power Query by Ad_id, Site_name and Impression_date. Aggregate by using the CountRows function.
Create a calculated table that contains Ad_id, Site_name and Impression_date.
Create a calculated measure that aggregates by using the COUNTROWS function.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: Create one-to-many relationships between the tables.
  • Option B: Group the Impressions query in Power Query by Ad_id, Site_name and Impression_date. Aggregate by using the CountRows function.

Why it is correct: grouping in Power Query reduces ~360 million rows to one row per ad/site/day with the count already computed (far smaller), and one-to-many relationships with dimensions allow analysis by campaign.

  • Official documentation: Group by - Microsoft Learn | Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Incorrect options:

  • Option C — Create a calculated table that contains Ad_id, Site_name and Impression_date. — Why it is incorrect: a calculated table duplicates data in the model and increases size.
  • Option D — Create a calculated measure that aggregates by using the COUNTROWS function. — Why it is incorrect: a COUNTROWS measure over the full table requires loading all ~360 million rows; it does not minimize size.

links.t: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling

q077.stem:
You import a Power BI dataset with the tables Date, Product and Product Inventory (25 million rows; columns such as DateKey, MovementDate, ProductKey, UnitCost…). Product Inventory relates to Date by DateKey and to Product by ProductKey.

You need to reduce the size of the data model without losing information. What should you do?
options: Change Summarization for DateKey to Don’t Summarize.
Remove the relationship between Date and Product Inventory.
Change the data type of UnitCost to Integer.
Remove MovementDate.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Official documentation: Data reduction techniques for Import modeling - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options:

  • Option A — Change Summarization for DateKey to Don’t Summarize. — Why it is incorrect: it only changes summarization behavior, not storage.

q078.stem:
You are enhancing a Power BI model with DAX calculations. You need a measure that returns the year-to-date total sales from the same date of the previous calendar year. Which DAX functions should you use? NOTE: each correct selection is worth one point.

Sales PYTD =
VAR startyear = STARTOFYEAR ( PREVIOUSYEAR ( 'Calendar'[Date] ) )
VAR enddate = LASTDATE ( Sales[Date] ) - 365
RETURN
  [A] ( [B] ( Sales[sales] ), [C] ( 'Calendar'[Date], startyear, enddate ) )

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • [A]: CALCULATE
  • [B]: SUM
  • [C]: DATESBETWEEN
  • [A] CALCULATE: changes the date context.
  • [B] SUM: adds Sales[sales] within that context.
  • [C] DATESBETWEEN: takes exactly (dates column, start, end), the three arguments shown: it returns the dates from the start of the previous year to the same date a year back. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR accepts only a dates column.

⚠️ Heads-up: the source text for the third box mentions SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, but the formula passes three arguments (column, start, end), which matches DATESBETWEEN; the latter is marked. Check it against the linked documentation.

  • Official documentation: DATESBETWEEN (DAX) - Microsoft Learn | SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR (DAX) - Microsoft Learn

You have a Power BI report named Orders that supports: total sales over time, the count of orders over time, and new and repeat customer counts. The model size is nearing the limit for a dataset in shared capacity.

Orders (OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, ProductID, UnitPrice, Quantity, Discount, SalesTotal) relates to Customers by CustomerID and to Date by OrderDate.

  • Removing CustomerID from Orders will reduce the model size while still supporting the current analysis.: No
  • Removing UnitPrice and Discount from Orders will reduce the model size while still supporting the current analysis.: Yes
  • 1 → No: grouping by those columns would lose line-level sales detail needed for total sales.
  • 2 → No: without CustomerID you cannot count new and repeat customers.
